from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
p.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
print('pages',len(r.pages))
text=[]
for i,page in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    t=page.extract_text()
    (p/f'page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(t)
    text.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n{t}')
(p/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(text))
print('\\n'.join(text[:3]))
PY"
/bin/bash -c 'cat tmp/pdfs/page-12.txt tmp/pdfs/page-13.txt tmp/pdfs/page-14.txt tmp/pdfs/page-15.txt tmp/pdfs/page-16.txt tmp/pdfs/page-17.txt'

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import re
from pathlib import Path
s=Path('tmp/pdfs/page-15.txt').read_text()
rows=[]
for line in s.splitlines():
    m=re.match(r'(.+?)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(.+)',line)
    if m:
        rows.append((m[1],float(m[2]),float(m[4])))
print('Table 11 occupation rows:',len(rows))
for name,group in [('male-stereotyped',rows[:20]),('female-stereotyped',rows[20:]),('all',rows)]:
    print(name, 'single mean signed SS',round(sum(r[1] for r in group)/len(group),3), 'paired mean signed SS',round(sum(r[2] for r in group)/len(group),3))
print('Independent balanced-gender baseline: Any =',1-0.5**2,'Both =',0.5**2)
for name,both,any_,reported in [('occupation',71.9,74.3,47.38),('power',57.9,59.7,18.98)]:
    print(name,'Figure 6 implied SS if all denominators match:',round(both+any_-100,2),'Table 1:',reported)
PY"

strengths: PST addresses a relevant gap in multimodal NLP evaluation: gender stereotypes can change when multiple people and their social roles must be represented together. Examining organizational power adds a useful perspective beyond occupation alone.

The occupational evaluation systematically combines 20 male-stereotyped and 20 female-stereotyped occupations in both positional orders. The appendices provide templates, identity lists, and detailed results that make the descriptive findings inspectable.

Human annotation uses three annotators per target and reports strong agreement, with Fleiss’ kappa of 0.88–0.92. Comparing automated classifiers against human judgments is useful, particularly given BLIP’s poor performance on paired images.

The results provide substantial evidence of increased adherence to conventional male stereotypes in the tested paired setting. FairCritic also offers a practical, understandable intervention whose reported aggregate improvements merit further investigation.
weaknesses: The central fairness interpretation exceeds what the metric establishes. SS averages signed stereotype adherence, allowing opposing biases to cancel. Table 1 illustrates this directly: single-person occupational scores of +50 for female-stereotyped occupations and −30 for male-stereotyped occupations become an overall score of 10, despite substantial imbalance. Consequently, low pooled SS does not establish either an unbiased baseline or FairCritic’s claimed near-perfect fairness. Post-mitigation distributions and absolute deviations from parity should be reported for individual occupations and roles, alongside joint outcomes.

The headline percentage and statistical comparisons require better calibration. Under independent, equally probable binary gender presentations, PST(Any) would classify 75% of images as stereotyped; therefore, the reported 74.3% is not independently evidence of bias or directly comparable with the single-person percentage. The high PST(Both) result is more informative. Meanwhile, only three single-person samples per identity support the occupation-level amplification analysis, with no confidence intervals or significance analysis to distinguish systematic changes from sampling variation.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified for reproducibility. Section 5.1 identifies the critic model and one-loop limit but does not adequately document complete critic inputs, images per critique, feedback insertion, or final evaluation sample counts. The relationship between images used for criticism and those used to estimate final fairness is unclear. A promised code release does not resolve these missing details in a central contribution.

The evidence does not establish FairCritic’s superiority over prompt interventions. Table 2 evaluates occupational intervention results on the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic over the broader occupational set. These are not matched comparisons. Evaluation on identical prompts and sampling budgets, including a fixed fairness-guidance baseline, is needed to isolate the benefit of adaptive visual feedback.

The evaluation does not establish that gender labels remain correctly associated with the requested roles. There is no reported audit of positional swaps, missing or extra people, occupation fidelity, or preservation of those properties after mitigation. Handling of the annotation option 'Cannot Identify' is also unspecified. Furthermore, the power template explicitly attaches the occupation only to the first role, weakening the intended comparison within the same industry.

Reporting and scope need tightening. The manuscript alternates between 944 and 1,952 constructed prompts, while only 216 power generations are evaluated; the distinction between the constructed inventory and evaluated subsets needs reconciliation. Conclusions should also remain specific to the tested English prompts and DALL-E 3. These scope limitations are manageable, but the unresolved measurement, comparison, and reproducibility issues require substantive revision before a positive Findings recommendation.
